content.summary: Welcome to Unit 9. In this reading mission, you will explore amazing natural places like deserts, mountains, and extreme environments around the world. You will practice reading short descriptive texts, learning how to compare different places using comparative and superlative adjectives, and talking about what animals can do in the wild.

linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming short paragraphs to get the main idea, and scanning for specific numbers, temperatures, and animal facts.

rules: Comparative adjectives: For short one-syllable adjectives, add -er and than. Example: hot becomes hotter than, big becomes bigger than.
Comparative adjectives: For long adjectives with two or more syllables, use more before the adjective and than after. Example: fascinating becomes more fascinating than.
Superlative adjectives: For short adjectives, use the before the adjective and add -est. Example: hot becomes the hottest.
Superlative adjectives: For long adjectives, use the most before the adjective. Example: dangerous becomes the most dangerous.
Can and can't for ability: Use subject + can or can't + base verb without 'to'. Example: Animals can run fast in the desert.
Questions with can: Start with Can + subject + verb. Example: Can camels live without water for a long time?

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often forget to use 'than' after comparative adjectives or 'the' before superlative adjectives.
commonTrap.wrong: Death Valley is hotter Death in California. Antarctica is most cold place.
commonTrap.correct: Death Valley is hotter than Death in California. Antarctica is the coldest place.

paragraphs: Our planet has many fascinating places. Some areas are very hot and dry, while others are freezing cold. For example, Death Valley in the United States is famous because it holds the record for the highest temperature on Earth. It is much hotter than most other deserts. During the summer, the temperature in Death Valley can reach over fifty degrees Celsius. People cannot live there easily, but some special plants and animals survive in the harsh bushland.

On the other side of the world, Antarctica is the coldest and windiest place on Earth. It is covered in thick ice and snow. Antarctica is more extreme than any other continent. Very few plants grow there, but amazing wildlife like penguins and seals live along the coast. Penguins cannot fly in the air, but they can swim very fast in the cold ocean. Exploring these natural wonders helps us understand the incredible power of nature.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Nature, Geography and Abilities

content.summary: Learn how to write about natural wonders and geographical features using comparative and superlative adjectives, and how to express abilities using can and can't.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Comparative Adjectives (Short)
blueprintItems.example: Mount Everest is higher than Mont Blanc.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Comparative Adjectives (Long)
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Verb + more + Adjective + than + Noun
blueprintItems.example: The Amazon rainforest is more dangerous than the local park.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Superlative Adjectives and Ability
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Verb + the + Adjective(-est / most) + Noun / Subject + can/can't + verb
blueprintItems.example: The Nile is the longest river in the world. Eagles can fly high.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize names of specific geographical places like mountains, rivers, and countries.
mechanicsRules.badExample: we visited mount everest and the nile river.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: We visited Mount Everest and the Nile River.
mechanicsRules.why: Specific mountains, rivers, oceans, and countries are proper nouns in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not double the consonant in comparative adjectives if the word ends with two consonants or two vowels before the consonant.
mechanicsRules.badExample: This river is deepger than that one.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: This river is deeper than that one.
mechanicsRules.why: Only single consonant words with a single vowel before it double the final letter.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use 'than' after a comparative adjective when comparing two things.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The desert is hotter the forest.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The desert is hotter than the forest.
mechanicsRules.why: The word 'than' is required to connect the two items being compared.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Superlative form for long adjectives uses 'the most' before the adjective.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the ideas into one sentence using 'because':

practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'because' to explain the reason.
targetAnswers: The desert is very hot during the day because water is difficult to find there.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'because' to connect an event or state with its cause.

practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf ˈænɪməls lɪv ɪn ðə ˈdezət, ðeɪ niːd ˈveri ˈlɪtl ˈwɔːtə/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ensure smooth transition between the conditional clause and the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice correct syllable stress on multi-syllable nature words.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Repeat after the prompt: temperature, fascinating, dangerous, and wildlife.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Temperature and fascinating are words with stress on the first syllable.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈtemprətʃə ənd ˈfæsɪneɪtɪŋ ɑː wɜːdz wɪð stres ɒn ðə fɜːst ˈsɪləbl/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Place strong emphasis on the first syllable of multi-syllable descriptive words.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice rising and falling intonation in conditional sentences.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say with rising intonation on the first part and falling on the second: If it is sunny, we will hike.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If it is sunny, we will hike in the park.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf ɪt ɪz ˈsʌni, wiː wɪl haɪk ɪn ðə pɑːk/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a rising pitch at the comma and a falling pitch at the end of the sentence.
